# A guide to the certificate library

Start with the [formal contract](README.md), then choose the construction whose hypotheses match your `(F, q, A)`. The library supplies reusable theorems; the accepted applications show how to discharge their geometric, algebraic and target-specific hypotheses. A similar-looking equation alone does not establish those hypotheses.

This is the current account of the available techniques. Each instance’s `why.md` retains the perspective just before its solution; its `solution.md` explains the proof and credits its sources.

## Assemble and transport certificates

| Task | Import and entry point | Obligations retained |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Check an explicit tuple | [`Constructions.Explicit`](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/Explicit.lean): `Verify.of_normalized` | Both normalized differential identities, exact integer degree balance, nonzero homogeneous `F` and `D`, source homogeneity, and coprimality. `Q` may be nonzero. |
| Prove denominator legality on a fiber | The same module: `relPrime_of_chart_specialization` | A chart with a left inverse, unit leading coefficient of the hypersurface **before** specialization, and a coprime specialized pair. |
| Add certificates | [`CertificateOperations`](lean/HodgeComputer/CertificateOperations.lean): `Verify.add`, `HasCertificate.add` | The same hypersurface and pole parameter. Denominators and quotient remainders may differ; the theorem constructs their product denominator. |
| Apply a sign involution | [`CoordinateChanges`](lean/HodgeComputer/CoordinateChanges.lean): `Verify.sign_change` | Each coordinate multiplier squares to one. The theorem transforms the field components as well as `F`, `A`, `D` and `Q`. |
| Reorder coordinates | The same module: `HasCertificate.rename` | An equivalence of the variable indices. This works in every ambient dimension. |
| Rescale a denominator and its numerator together | [`HodgeTestbed.Algebra`](lean/HodgeTestbed/Algebra.lean): `Equations.scale` | The quotient scales by the square of the multiplier. Legality and grading of the new denominator are separate obligations. |

The 41 small explicit witnesses now share their assembly and legality interface. They still prove their own polynomial identities and bind the exact displayed tuple to the protected witness. Their contact, cofactor and norm interpretations are developed in [Chapter 2](../docs/02-explicit-constructions.md); a checked individual tuple is not a general existence theorem for that interpretation.

For the Fermat sextic, [`Constructions.Fermat`](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/Fermat.lean) supplies the stronger theorem `HodgeComputer.Fermat.certificate`: every homogeneous odd source at `q = 1` or `q = 2` has a certificate. Its subset Euler construction and finite subset assertion are proved in Lean. The original `fermat-q2` application retains its own displayed witness.

## Construct primitives and clear them

| Construction | Library | What remains with an application |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fermat cover and moving conic for the fixed holdout sextic | [HoldoutCover](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/HoldoutCover/README.md), especially `HoldoutGeneralization.certificate_of_source_pair` | The quotient-source identity, its normal derivative identity and trace-zero correction. Different quotient equations need their own geometry. |
| Lift an incidence seed and integrate on a polynomial curve | [PolynomialCurves](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/PolynomialCurves/README.md) | A nonsingular incidence seed, finite extension, dominance, polynomial normal and exact source transport. |
| Contract two supplied elliptic companion primitives | [EllipticCompanions](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/EllipticCompanions/README.md), `CrossedElliptic.product_divergence` | The companion equations and scalar primitives, independence, embeddings and physical closure. The elliptic curve here is the Fermat cubic. |
| Integrate a third-order pole along a polynomial family | [HigherResidues](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/HigherResidues/README.md) | The polynomial family, actual numerator/determinant jets, finite descent and certificate closure. |
| Construct a contact field over a finite algebra | [FiniteAlgebra](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/FiniteAlgebra/README.md) | The contact line, finite algebra, source-span calculation, specialization and denominator checks. |
| Correct a cubic-surface field from pole one to pole two | [CubicSurfaces](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/CubicSurfaces/README.md), `Q2Reduction.q2_equations` | A homogeneous cubic, a Jacobian representation of the source and a strict primitive for the resulting divergence. |
| Correct and homogenize a rational field | [RationalFields](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/RationalFields/README.md) | Commuting derivations, a normal field and primitive, actual chart rules, and the Euler degree condition. |

Several broadly reusable steps still live under `HoldoutCover`: `PolynomialNormal` constructs normals from invertible coefficient matrices; `FiniteTrace` descends primitives; `ResidueClearing`, `FiniteResidueClearing` and `HomogeneousCertificate` clear and grade their polynomial witnesses. Those modules expose explicit hypotheses. In contrast, `GeneralizedCover` fixes the holdout hypersurface. The directory name does not make every theorem a result about arbitrary hypersurfaces.

## Cubic covariants and moving maps

There are four distinct coefficient families:

- [BinaryCubic](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/BinaryCubic/README.md) supplies four-coefficient Hessian/discriminant identities and the radial cancellation used by the dense two-ternary witness.
- [CyclicCubic](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/CyclicCubic/README.md) treats `a x³ + b y³ + c z³ + d x²y + e y²z + f z²x`.
- [TransitiveCubic](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/TransitiveCubic/README.md) replaces the last monomial by `f x²z`. Its optional `Shear` module handles a supplied quadratic coordinate reduction.
- [PolarCubic](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/PolarCubic/README.md) treats `a x³ + b y³ + c z³ + d x²y + e y²z + f xy²` and its first-order `2kxyz` perturbation.

The cubic applications import their coefficient identities directly. These families have different covariants; substituting one family’s tables into another would change the mathematics.

All four Jacobian applications use the common dual-number chain rule and first variations in [`ResidueTransport.FirstJets`](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/ResidueTransport/FirstJets.lean). Their remaining `CubicJetCalculus.lean` files prove the family-specific cleared differential and cubic variation. [ResidueTransport](lean/HodgeComputer/Constructions/ResidueTransport/README.md) also supplies density changes, moving-map corrections, normal changes and the coordinate-independence criterion. Constructing the Jacobian primitive and checking the physical source remain application obligations.

## Reading and extending the library

Read a module’s hypotheses before adapting its worked application. Keep a new target’s constants, incidence seeds and final protected binding together in its instance folder. The shared implementation is the place for parameterized identities and established constructions, with attribution to the proofs from which they came. [MAINTAINING.md](../MAINTAINING.md) describes shared-module kernel replay and verification of dependent applications.

# Sextic fourfolds with an involution

These chapters study the generalized Hodge conjecture for the involution-invariant middle cohomology of a smooth sextic fourfold. The central question is whether that cohomology is supported on a divisor. Rational differential forms turn the support condition into an algebraic certificate equation; correspondences and quotient geometry establish it for several families.

The treatment is organized around general mechanisms and their hypotheses. Examples illustrate those mechanisms, while the case of a general globally \(Y\)-even sextic remains the motivating open problem.

## Reading order

The intended reader knows basic algebraic geometry, differential forms and Hodge decomposition. Chapter 1 identifies the geometric and algebraic formulations. Chapter 2 develops the algebraic calculus of rational primitives, and Chapter 2A works out the relation between binary contacts and Jacobian torsion. Chapters 3–3C establish geometric support theorems and their applications to complete families. Chapter 4 studies coefficient spaces, finite symmetries and deformation, and Chapter 5 develops exact coefficient methods. Foundational results from the literature are cited where they enter.

| Chapter | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| [1. From invariant cohomology to rational certificates](#technical-information/certificates) | The key equation, normalization, prescribed support, trace and coefficient descent |
| [2. Algebraic constructions and residue transport](#technical-information/explicit-constructions) | Cofactor transport, cyclic suspension, closed currents and variation of rational primitives |
| [2A. Binary sextics and torsion contacts](#technical-information/binary-blocks) | Genus-two three-torsion, Wronskian spanning theorems and a binary-block construction |
| [3. Geometric support](#technical-information/geometric-support) | Gysin maps, finite-group projectors, Fano and surface fibrations, and supported projectors in families |
| [3A. Split sextics and K3 surfaces](#technical-information/split-and-k3) | Elliptic companions, polarized splitting and the algebraic Kuga–Satake criterion |
| [3B. Weighted threefolds and two-reflection sextics](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds) | Norm-contact curves, Abel–Jacobi residues, finite-jet spanning and two-reflection support |
| [3C. Quadratic nets and pair correspondences](#technical-information/quadratic-nets) | Finite-cover incidence, discriminant conics, Fano threefolds and support without extra reflections |
| [4. Families, representations and deformation](#technical-information/known-locus) | Invariant sectors, coefficient families, generic-target reduction and limits of quotient methods |
| [5. Computing and checking certificates](#technical-information/computation) | Complete coefficient systems, incidence lifting and the exact polynomial criterion |

The geometric constructions combine supported images of algebraic correspondences. In Chapter 3B, Fano reflection quotients and norm-contact curves on weighted threefolds serve complementary sectors. In Chapter 3C, a finite map defined by three ternary quadrics and the six joining lines of its four-point fibers recover the entire invariant cohomology. The diagonal net gives the three-reflection case as a corollary. The two-reflection theorem has a different coefficient scope and remains necessary for general crossed splittings and binary-block families. Chapter 2A retains their independent contact construction and its Wronskian spanning results. Chapter 4 applies deck/exchange descent to the full cyclic-six coefficient family.

## Notation

We use \(Z=(X_0,X_1,X_2,Y_0,Y_1,Y_2)\), \(\tau(X,Y)=(X,-Y)\), and \(X=V(F)\subset\mathbb P^5\) for the fourfold. “\(Y\)-even” means even total degree in the three \(Y\) variables, unless individual coordinate reflections are stated. A residue numerator \(A\) is \(Y\)-odd because the projective volume form changes sign under \(\tau\). In the general certificate equation, \(n\) is the ambient projective dimension and \(d=\deg F\); here \(n=5,d=6\). The pole parameter \(q\) is distinct from the denominator degree \(\deg D\).

Over six complex variables \(X_0,X_1,X_2,Y_0,Y_1,Y_2\), consider a smooth sextic fourfold \(X\subset\mathbb P^5\) defined by a homogeneous sextic polynomial \(F(X_0,X_1,X_2,Y_0,Y_1,Y_2)\) invariant under the involution

\[
\iota:(X_0,X_1,X_2,Y_0,Y_1,Y_2)\mapsto(X_0,X_1,X_2,-Y_0,-Y_1,-Y_2).
\]
The involution \(\iota\) induces an action on \(X\), and so also on \(H^4(X,\mathbb Q)\). As noted by [Voisin](https://www.ms.u-tokyo.ac.jp/journal/abstract_e/jms220116_e.html), the Hodge substructure \(H\subset H^4(X,\mathbb Q)\) *fixed* by the induced action \(\iota^*\) has *Hodge coniveau* 1. Indeed, \(\iota^*\) acts as \(-1\) on the nowhere-vanishing Calabi–Yau form \(\omega\in H^{4,0}(X)\).

The generalized Hodge conjecture thus predicts that \(H\)’s *geometric coniveau* should also be 1; that is, there should exist a divisor \(Y\subset X\) such that

\[
H\subset\ker\left(H^4(X,\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H^4(X\setminus Y,\mathbb Q)\right).
\]
This particular instance of the GHC is interesting in its own right. Further, as [Voisin](https://www.ms.u-tokyo.ac.jp/journal/abstract_e/jms220116_e.html) points out, if true for general smooth even \(F\), it would imply [Voisin’s conjecture](https://www.cmls.polytechnique.fr/perso/voisin/Articlesweb/symmetriccycles1.pdf) for K3 surfaces that are double covers of \(\mathbb P^2\) ramified over a sextic curve.

> **Parity convention.** In these coordinates, “even” and “odd” mean even and odd total degree in the three \(Y\) variables.

In a recent work, [Diamond](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29157) shows that the prediction of the GHC as regards \(H\subset H^4(X,\mathbb Q)\) is *equivalent* to a purely algebraic one. For \(F\) given as above—an even homogeneous sextic whose vanishing locus is smooth—is it true that, for each \(q\in\{1,2\}\) and each *odd* monomial \(A\) of degree \(6\cdot q\), there exists a vector field \(v=(v_0,\ldots,v_5)\) whose components are homogeneous *rational* functions of total degree \(6\cdot q-5\), and whose common denominator \(D\) is not divisible by \(F\), such that

\[
F^{q+1}\;\bigm|\;A-q\cdot\mathrm dF(v)+F\cdot\operatorname{div}(v)?
\]
Divisibility is interpreted in \(\mathbb C[X_0,X_1,X_2,Y_0,Y_1,Y_2]_{(F)}\).

This algebraic formulation makes divisor support accessible through rational differential forms and exact polynomial identities.

The book proves support on several complete coefficient families. [Chapter 3C](#technical-information/quadratic-nets) treats every smooth sextic \(F(X,Y)=G(X,Q_0(Y),Q_1(Y),Q_2(Y))\) obtained from three ternary quadrics: point-pair incidence combines a weighted Fano quotient with a family of Fano threefolds. This includes the three-reflection family through the diagonal net. The complementary [two-reflection theorem](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds) combines Fano quotients with norm-contact curves and includes the full \(4+2\) split family with binary block \((X_2,Y_2)\). [Chapter 4](#technical-information/known-locus) compares their coefficient spaces and treats further finite-symmetry families. The general even-sextic case remains open.
